newsitem.title: UK: Orange Order parade to go ahead after protests.
newsitem.headline: Orange Order parade to go ahead after protests.

text.p: Northern Ireland's police chief said on Sunday that a disputed Orange Order parade would be allowed along Portadown's Garvaghy road, scene of violent protests by Catholics who want it stopped.

Ronnie Flanagan, head of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, told a hastily-convened news conference that the decision, which ended days of deadlock, was taken to avert a repeat of days of violent standoff which surrounded the same parade last year.

He said it was taken in conjunction with Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, late on Saturday night after efforts to reach a compromise between the Protestant Order and Garvaghy road residents failed.

Flanagan said the authorites risked a re-run of last year's Protestant rioting if the march was banned and Catholic fury if it was allowed to follow its chosen route down the half-mile (one km) Garvaghy road area on the edge of Portadown.
"The choice I was left with was a simple, stark choice in terms of balancing two evils, each evil bound to bring about serious violence," he said.
"I apologise to the people of Garvaghy Road for the gross inconvenience this has caused and assure them that the level of inconvenience will be for as short a period as possible."

He said Orange Order members would be allowed to walk down the Garvaghy road but, in a concession to Irish nationalists, only one band would be permitted to head the march. "I want to see this march over as quickly as possible," he added.
Catholics of the Garvaghy road were furious. "We have been betrayed," said one middle-aged woman.

In Dublin, a spokesman for Prime Minister Bertie Ahern's government, which wanted the parade rerouted to avoid offending Catholics, said it learned of the move "with deep disappointment." The march was scheduled to start at 1000 a.m. (0900 GMT) from Portadown centre and follow a route to a tiny Protestant church at Drumcree for prayers before turning back towards Portadown along the Garvaghy road.
Hundreds of police backed by British troops seized control of the Garvaghy road before dawn in one of the biggest security operations mounted in Northern Ireland for decades.
Residents threw rocks and petrol bombs at security forces and a dozen people were injured by plastic bullets as residents tried to drive back columns of riot police.
A solid line of armoured grey police jeeps lined the road bumper to bumper protecting hundreds of riot police with shields, helmets and batons.
Around the town British troops in armoured cars armed with a variety of automatic weapons guarded the police operation and mounted checkpoints at all roads leading to the southern town.
One year ago police prevented the marchers going through the Catholic enclave but changed their decision after days of Protestant rioting and sparked Catholic fury instead.

At the other end of the province, police clashed overnight with Catholic residents of the small town of Bellaghy who want an Orange Order parade there on Monday stopped. One policeman was reported injured.

Dozens more Protestant parades are to be staged this week in the build-up to the 12th of July, the most cherished date in the Orange calendar which marks a 17th century Protestant victory over Britain's last Catholic king.
Gerry Adams, president of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, said in a statement: "The attack on the people of the Garvaghy road is totally unjustifiable."
His party, which shares the underground Irish Republican Army's goal of ending British rule of Northern Ireland, wanted the march banned.
